understanding.title: Understanding UUIDs
understanding.p1: A UUID — Universally Unique Identifier — is a 128-bit value written as 32 hexadecimal characters split into five groups of 8-4-4-4-12. With its four hyphens it is exactly 36 characters long, which is why you see it everywhere from database columns to log lines.
understanding.p2: The reason UUIDs exist is coordination-free uniqueness. Any process, on any machine, can mint one without asking a central authority for the next number in a sequence. Two services that have never spoken to each other can generate identifiers all day and still never collide in practice.
understanding.p3: The layout is standardised by RFC 9562, which superseded the long-serving RFC 4122. Two fields are fixed by the spec: the version nibble, which is the first character of the third group, and the variant bits at the start of the fourth group. Everything else is filled by the version's own algorithm.

why.title: Why use UUIDs
why.p1: Auto-incrementing integers are compact and readable, but they force every writer through a single source of truth. UUIDs remove that bottleneck: a mobile client can create records while offline, a queue consumer can assign ids before the row exists, and two shards can merge without renumbering anything.
why.p2: They are also safer to expose. A sequential id in a URL quietly publishes how many records you have and lets anyone walk your dataset by counting upwards. A UUID reveals neither.
why.p3: The trade-offs are real and worth naming. A UUID takes 16 bytes against 8 for a bigint, and 36 bytes if you store the text form. Fully random v4 values also scatter B-tree inserts across the whole index, which hurts write throughput on large tables. Version 7 was standardised precisely to solve that second problem.

types.title: Types of UUIDs
types.intro: RFC 9562 defines eight versions. Three of them cover almost every real use case, and those are the three this generator produces.
types.tableCaption: Comparison of the UUID versions offered by ToolForge
types.v1BestFor: Legacy systems that already expect v1
types.v4BestFor: General purpose ids, tokens, correlation keys
types.v7BestFor: Database primary keys and event streams
types.others: The remaining versions are niche: v3 and v5 hash a name into a namespace deterministically, v6 reorders the v1 timestamp so it sorts correctly, and v8 is a deliberately open slot for vendor-specific layouts.

howItWorks.title: How our generator works
howItWorks.p1: Every identifier on this page is produced by the Web Crypto API — specifically crypto.getRandomValues, the same cryptographically secure source your browser uses for TLS. There is no server call, no queue, and no fallback to Math.random.
howItWorks.p2: Version 7 gets one extra guarantee. When several ids are minted inside the same millisecond, the twelve rand_a bits are used as a dedicated counter rather than random noise, following the monotonicity method in RFC 9562. A batch of 500 therefore comes back in strictly ascending order.
howItWorks.p3: Because the work happens locally, the values you see were never transmitted, never logged, and never stored. Load the page once and it keeps working with the network switched off. The batch size is capped at 500 so a single generation stays imperceptible even on a low-powered device.

useCases.title: Use cases
useCases.p1: The most common use is a primary key. Version 7 is the better choice here: it keeps inserts clustered at the right edge of the index the way a sequence would, while still being generated by the client.
useCases.p2: Idempotency keys are the second big one. Attach a fresh UUID to a payment or a webhook retry and the receiving service can safely discard duplicates without any shared state.
useCases.p3: Beyond persistence, UUIDs are the default for correlation and trace ids that stitch a request together across services, for object-storage keys that must not collide between uploaders, and for seeded test fixtures where a readable, guaranteed-unique value beats a hand-written string.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Can two UUIDs ever be the same?
faq.a1: Mathematically yes, practically no. A version 4 UUID has 122 random bits. You would need to generate roughly 2.7 × 10^18 of them before reaching a one-in-a-billion chance of a single collision.
faq.a2: Version 7 for anything stored in an indexed column, version 4 for everything else. Only reach for version 1 when an existing system already depends on its layout.
faq.q3: Are these UUIDs safe to use as security tokens?
faq.a3: Version 4 UUIDs from this page are backed by a cryptographically secure random source, so they are unguessable. Versions 1 and 7 embed a readable timestamp, so treat them as identifiers rather than secrets.
faq.q4: Is anything I generate sent to your servers?
faq.a4: No. The generator is client-side JavaScript. The page makes no network request while generating, and nothing you copy or download is ever transmitted.

understanding.title: Understanding Base64
understanding.p1: Base64 is a binary-to-text encoding. It takes arbitrary bytes and rewrites them using 64 printable ASCII characters — A–Z, a–z, 0–9 and two symbols — so the data can travel through any channel that only understands text.
understanding.p2: The scheme works in groups of three bytes. Twenty-four bits divide evenly into four six-bit numbers, and each number selects one character from the alphabet. When the input does not divide by three, the final group is padded with one or two = characters so the output length stays a multiple of four.
understanding.p3: That regularity is the whole point. Base64 is neither compression nor encryption: anyone can decode it, and the result is always about a third larger than what went in. It exists so bytes survive a trip through systems that would otherwise mangle them.

why.title: Why encode to Base64
why.p1: Plenty of formats are text-only by design. Email bodies, JSON payloads, XML documents, HTTP headers and YAML files all expect characters rather than raw bytes. Drop a PNG straight into any of them and the first byte outside the printable range breaks the parser.
why.p2: Base64 gives those bytes a safe disguise. An image can be embedded in a stylesheet, a certificate can be pasted into a config file, and a binary attachment can move through a mail server written decades ago — none of which needed changing.
why.p3: The cost is size and readability. A megabyte of input becomes roughly 1.37 MB of output, and no human can read it. Reach for it when the channel demands text, not out of habit: if you control both ends and they speak binary, send binary.

variants.title: Variants of Base64
variants.intro: The variants in daily use differ in only two places — the last two characters of the alphabet, and whether the output carries its padding.
variants.tableCaption: Comparison of the Base64 variants ToolForge produces
variants.standardBestFor: MIME, email, and most APIs and libraries
variants.dataUriBestFor: Inline images in CSS, HTML, and Markdown
variants.others: RFC 4648 also defines base32 and base16 for cases where case-insensitivity matters more than density. Despite the different name, base64url is the same encoding — only the two final symbols change, so a decoder that accepts both, like this one, never has to be told which it is reading.

options.title: Every option, and when to use it
options.intro: The defaults — UTF-8, standard alphabet, padded, one continuous payload — are what you want most of the time. The rest of the controls exist for the cases where the receiving system is stricter, older, or expects a particular shape.
options.tableCaption: What each converter option does and when it is worth turning on
options.charsetDoes: Decides how text becomes bytes when encoding, and how bytes become text when decoding.
options.charsetWhen: The data is not UTF-8 — a Windows-1252 spreadsheet export, an ISO-8859-2 dump, a Shift_JIS log.
options.newlineDoes: Rewrites every line break in the result to LF, CRLF, or CR, whatever the input used.
options.newlineWhen: The receiver is strict about it, such as Windows tooling or a protocol that demands CRLF.
options.perLineDoes: Converts one line at a time instead of treating the whole box as a single payload.
options.perLineWhen: You have a list — one token, id, or string per line — and want a result for each.
options.urlSafeDoes: Swaps the final two alphabet characters, + and /, for - and _.
options.urlSafeWhen: The result goes into a URL, a filename, or a JWT segment.
options.paddingDoes: Adds the trailing = characters so the length is always a multiple of four.
options.paddingWhen: The receiver expects it. Leave it off for base64url, which conventionally drops it.
options.wrapDoes: Folds the encoded output into 76-character lines.
options.wrapWhen: You are writing a MIME body or a PEM-style block, both of which expect wrapped text.
options.dataUriDoes: Prefixes the payload with data:'<type>';base64, using the file's own media type.
options.dataUriWhen: The result is going straight into CSS, HTML, or Markdown as an inline asset.
options.charsetNote: Two things about character sets are worth knowing. Encoding can only write a set this page can also invert, so the multi-byte East Asian sets — Shift_JIS, GBK, GB18030, Big5, EUC-JP, EUC-KR — are offered when decoding but not when encoding. And a set narrower than your text will say so: type an emoji with ASCII selected and you get the exact position that cannot be written, rather than a silently corrupted byte.
options.defaultsNote: The options also constrain each other, and the interface follows suit rather than producing something broken. A data URI describes one continuous standard-alphabet payload, so switching on URL-safe, line wrapping, or per-line conversion greys it out. Encoding a file ignores the character set and line endings entirely, because a file is already bytes and has no line structure to normalise.

howItWorks.title: How our converter works
howItWorks.p1: Everything on this page runs on your device. The encoder walks the input three bytes at a time and emits four characters per group; the decoder does the reverse, folding four characters back into three bytes. There is no server call and nothing is stored.
howItWorks.p2: Text becomes bytes before it is encoded, and which bytes depends on the source character set. UTF-8 is the default and the only one that carries every script; pick Windows-1252 or ISO-8859-2 and anything outside that set is reported rather than silently mangled. Decoding applies the same choice in reverse, so a payload written in Shift_JIS reads back as Japanese instead of mojibake. Converters built on the browser's own btoa can do none of this — btoa throws on any character above U+00FF.
howItWorks.p3: The decoder is deliberately forgiving. It reads either alphabet, ignores line breaks and spaces, tolerates missing padding, and strips a data: URI header when it finds one. What it will not do is guess: a character outside the alphabet is reported with its exact position instead of being silently dropped. Lists can be converted a line at a time, line endings rewritten to LF, CRLF or CR, and encoded output folded at 76 characters the way a MIME body expects.

useCases.title: Use cases
useCases.p1: Data URIs are the most visible use. A small icon encoded into a stylesheet saves a request, and an inline preview needs no upload at all.
useCases.p2: Credentials and keys are the second. HTTP Basic auth is a Base64 pair, JWT headers and payloads are base64url, and PEM certificates are Base64 wrapped at 64 columns between BEGIN and END lines.
useCases.p3: Beyond that: attaching files to a JSON API with no multipart endpoint, storing small blobs in a column that only accepts text, and moving binaries through logs, webhooks, or a paste into a terminal.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is Base64 a form of encryption?
faq.a1: No. It is a reversible encoding with no key, and every language ships a decoder. Anything you encode is readable by anyone who receives it, so never use it to hide a secret.
faq.q2: Why is the encoded output bigger than my file?
faq.a2: Every three bytes become four characters, so the output grows by about a third, plus up to two padding characters. That overhead is inherent to the encoding and cannot be tuned away.
faq.q3: What is the difference between Base64 and base64url?
faq.a3: Only the last two characters of the alphabet. Standard Base64 uses + and /, both of which mean something inside a URL; base64url swaps them for - and _ and usually drops the = padding. Turn on URL-safe above to produce it.
faq.a4: No. Files are read with the browser's File API and converted on your device. The page makes no network request while converting, and nothing you paste, open, or download is ever transmitted.
faq.q5: Which character set should I pick?
faq.a5: UTF-8 unless you know otherwise — it covers every script and is what the modern web assumes. Reach for another only when the data itself predates that: a Windows-1252 spreadsheet export, an ISO-8859-2 dump, a Shift_JIS log. If a decode comes back as mojibake, the destination character set is usually the thing to change.
faq.q6: Why does my output have line breaks in it?
faq.a6: Either “Split at 76 chars” is on, which folds the payload the way a MIME body needs, or “Each line separately” is on, which emits one result per input line. Both are off by default; turning them off gives you a single continuous string again.

understanding.title: What a JSON Web Token actually is
understanding.p1: A JSON Web Token is a compact, URL-safe way to carry a set of claims — statements such as who a user is, what they may do, and when the statement stops being true. RFC 7519 defines the format; RFC 7515 defines the signature that makes it trustworthy.
understanding.p2: The value you paste into this tool is a JWS: three base64url-encoded parts joined by dots. The first two are JSON objects, plainly readable by anyone. The third is a signature over the first two, which is what turns a readable blob into something a server can rely on.
understanding.p3: That split explains most of what people find surprising about JWTs. Reading one requires nothing. Trusting one requires the key. The tool above keeps those two jobs visibly separate, because conflating them is where real systems go wrong.

anatomy.title: The three parts
anatomy.intro: Each part is base64url with its padding stripped, so a token survives being pasted into a URL, a header, or a cookie without further escaping.
anatomy.tableCaption: The three segments of a JWS and what each contributes
anatomy.headerHolds: How the token was signed: alg, typ, and often a kid naming the key.
anatomy.headerSigned: Yes — altering it invalidates the signature.
anatomy.payloadHolds: The claims themselves: registered ones such as sub and exp, plus anything the issuer adds.
anatomy.payloadSigned: Yes — altering it invalidates the signature.
anatomy.signatureHolds: The MAC or signature over the first two parts, joined by a dot.
anatomy.encoding: Base64url is an encoding, not a cipher. Decoding a payload takes no key and no permission — which is why the same claim data must never include anything you would not print in a log.

claims.title: The registered claims
claims.intro: RFC 7519 reserves seven claim names. None is mandatory, but a token that omits exp has no way to stop being valid, and one that omits iss and aud is hard to scope to a single service.
claims.tableCaption: Registered JWT claims and what each carries
claims.issDetail: Identifies who minted the token, so a verifier can pick the right key and reject tokens from anyone else.
claims.subDetail: Identifies the principal the claims are about — usually a user id, and unique within the issuer.
claims.audDetail: Names the recipients the token is for. A service that finds itself absent from aud must reject the token.
claims.expDetail: Seconds since the Unix epoch after which the token must be rejected. The single most important claim to include.
claims.nbfDetail: Seconds since the epoch before which the token must be rejected — useful for credentials issued ahead of time.
claims.iatDetail: When the token was created. Lets a verifier reject anything older than it is willing to accept, independently of exp.
claims.jtiDetail: A unique identifier for the token, so a replayed copy can be spotted and refused.
claims.privateClaims: Everything else is a public or private claim, named by whoever issues the token. Prefixing your own claims with a URI or a short vendor namespace keeps them from colliding with a future registered name.

algorithms.title: Signing algorithms
algorithms.intro: The alg header names one entry from the JOSE registry. The families differ in what the verifier needs to hold: a copy of the signing secret, or only a public key.
algorithms.tableCaption: JWS algorithm families supported by this tool
algorithms.hmacKey: One shared secret, used to sign and to verify.
algorithms.hmacWhen: The same service issues and checks the token, so there is no third party to keep a secret from.
algorithms.rsaKey: Private key to sign, public key to verify.
algorithms.rsaWhen: Verifiers are separate services, or outside your control, and you need the widest possible library support.
algorithms.rsaPssKey: Private key to sign, public key to verify.
algorithms.rsaPssWhen: You want the modern RSA padding and control both ends well enough to know PS is supported.
algorithms.ecdsaKey: Private key to sign, public key to verify.
algorithms.ecdsaWhen: You want asymmetric verification with far smaller keys and signatures than RSA.
algorithms.eddsaKey: Private key to sign, public key to verify.
algorithms.eddsaWhen: You control the stack and want the fastest, simplest modern signature — Ed25519 under the hood.
algorithms.noneNote: The registry also lists none, an unsigned token. This tool decodes those and flags them loudly, but will not issue one: a token with no signature is a claim with no evidence, and verifiers that trusted the header's algorithm are exactly how that became a documented attack.
algorithms.sizeNote: For HMAC, RFC 7518 asks for a key at least as long as the hash: 32 bytes for HS256, 48 for HS384, 64 for HS512. A shorter secret still produces a valid-looking token, which is why the workbench points it out rather than quietly accepting it.

verifying.title: How verification actually works
verifying.p1: Verifying recomputes the signature over the first two segments, exactly as they appear in the token, and compares it with the third. This is why the tool signs a compacted copy of your payload rather than the indented text in the editor: the bytes that were signed are the bytes that must be checked.
verifying.p2: The order matters. Check the structure, then the signature, then the claims. A token whose exp has passed is worth rejecting, but only after you know the exp you are reading is one the issuer actually wrote.
verifying.p3: The rule worth carrying away: never verify with the algorithm the token asks for. Pass your verifier an explicit list of algorithms you accept. A verifier that reads alg from the header can be handed an RS256 token rewritten as HS256, signed with the very public key it publishes — the public key becomes the HMAC secret, and the forgery verifies.
verifying.p4: That is why the decoder above shows an expected-algorithm control instead of silently following the header. It starts from what the token declares, then checks against your choice, and says so plainly when the two disagree.

options.title: Every control on this page
options.intro: The workbench has two directions and a small set of controls shared between them.
options.tableCaption: Controls in the JWT workbench, what each does, and when to use it
options.modeDoes: Switches between reading a token and signing one.
options.modeWhen: You have a token to inspect, or claims you want to turn into one.
options.exampleDoes: Signs a sample token, minting a throwaway key pair for the asymmetric families.
options.exampleWhen: You want to try RS, PS, ES or EdDSA without having a key pair to hand.
options.viewDoes: Swaps the decoded panels between raw JSON and a table that names each claim and dates the time claims.
options.viewWhen: You want the exact bytes, or you want to know what exp is actually saying.
options.expectedAlgorithmDoes: Fixes the one algorithm the signature is checked against, and swaps the key box to match.
options.expectedAlgorithmWhen: Always. Leave it on the token's own value to confirm a signature; change it to see a mismatch reported.
options.secretDoes: Holds the shared secret for the HMAC family.
options.secretWhen: The token's alg starts with HS.
options.base64urlDoes: Decodes the secret from base64 to raw bytes before use, instead of taking the text's own bytes.
options.base64urlWhen: Your issuer stores its secret as base64 — most generated secrets are. Getting this wrong is the usual cause of a signature that will not match.
options.pemDoes: Accepts a public key or certificate for verifying, and a PKCS#8 private key for signing.
options.pemWhen: The token's alg starts with RS, PS, ES, or is EdDSA.
options.downloadDoes: Saves the decoded header, payload and signature as JSON, or the signed token as a text file.
options.downloadWhen: You want the result in a fixture file rather than on the clipboard.
options.headerOwnsAlg: In the encoder, the header is the single source of truth for alg. The algorithm select writes into it rather than sitting beside it, so there is never a second value to fall out of step — edit the header directly and the signing algorithm follows.
options.noTokenParam: There is deliberately no way to put a token in this page's URL. A JWT is a bearer credential, and a URL ends up in browser history, proxy logs, server access logs, and the Referer header of every outbound link. Only the mode and the algorithm travel in a link.

pitfalls.title: What goes wrong in practice
pitfalls.p1: Encoded is not encrypted. Every claim in a JWT is readable by anyone who holds the token, including the user it was issued to. Email addresses, internal ids and role names all leak by design; passwords and API keys in a payload are a live incident, not a code-review nit.
pitfalls.p2: Signatures do not expire on their own. A token stays valid until its exp passes, and there is no way to call it back before then. Anything you might need to withdraw quickly — a session, an elevated role — needs either a short life or a revocation list the verifier actually checks.
pitfalls.p3: The algorithm is an attacker-controlled field until you pin it. Accept an explicit allowlist in your verifier and treat everything else, none included, as a rejected token.
pitfalls.p4: Header parameters that name a key are equally attacker-controlled. jku, jwk and x5u ask a verifier to fetch or trust key material chosen by the token; unless you are certain your library ignores them, assume a token carrying them is trying something.
pitfalls.p5: Where the token lives matters as much as what is in it. localStorage is readable by any script on the page, which turns one cross-site scripting bug into stolen credentials. Prefer a cookie with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite set, and keep the lifetime short.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.a1: No. Decoding, signing and verification all run in your browser through the Web Crypto API. There is no request to any server, which is also why the tool works with the network switched off. The page has no way to put a token in its URL either, so nothing lands in browser history or server logs.
faq.a2: No. A standard JWT is signed, which proves it was not altered — it does not hide anything. The header and payload are base64url, an encoding anyone can reverse in one line of code. If the contents must stay private, you want a JWE, the five-part encrypted format, which this tool identifies but cannot open.
faq.q3: Why does my signature not verify?
faq.a3: Usually the secret is right but its form is wrong. Many issuers store an HMAC secret as base64, and signing with the letters of that string is not the same as signing with the bytes it encodes — the Base64url encoded switch decides which one is used. Otherwise: check that the expected algorithm matches the header, that an RSA or EC key is the public half rather than the private one, and that the token was not truncated in a copy.
faq.q4: Can I create a token with alg: none?
faq.a4: The decoder reads them and flags them, but the encoder will not issue one. An unsigned token is a set of claims with no evidence behind them, and verifiers that trusted the header's algorithm turned that into a documented attack. If you need one to test a defence, produce it deliberately in your own test code rather than from a public page.
faq.q5: What key format does the tool accept?
faq.a5: HMAC takes a plain secret, optionally base64url encoded. The RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA families take PEM: a PUBLIC KEY or CERTIFICATE block for verifying, and a PKCS#8 PRIVATE KEY block for signing. PKCS#1 blocks, the ones beginning BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY, are not supported by Web Crypto — convert with openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt -in key.pem.
faq.q6: How long should a token live?
faq.a6: Short enough that a stolen copy stops working before it is useful, and long enough not to fight your refresh flow. Minutes for an access token is a common answer; days is a decision to make deliberately. The workbench flags a token with no exp at all, and notes one whose expiry is far enough out that revocation becomes your only way to withdraw it.
